title: Top requests over the last 24 hours
description: Find the N most frequent search strings, requested keys, or other request identities across hundreds of machines over the trailing 24 hours, with efficient computation and network use.
focus: source collection, lossless local combining, key-based partitioning, rolling expiration, exact Top-N merging, and replay-safe recovery.

children.value: Distributed frequency counting, not just a heap
Which requests occurred most often in the last 24 hours?

Collect from hundreds of serving machines, count every request identity correctly across the fleet, expire yesterday's traffic, and serve the Top-N without funneling the entire workload through one counter.
Based on the supplied distributed Top-N prompt and scoring notes. The example scale, snapshot cadence, and limits are proposed interview assumptions, not hidden requirements.

Combine counts near the sources, partition by request identity, maintain each key's complete rolling total, rank within those key partitions, then merge only their Top-N candidates at one common cutoff.

Never discard non-winning keys at the source machines. Never confuse an exact result for a minute-aligned snapshot with an exact window ending at this arbitrary second. Those are the two most important boundaries to defend.
A close relative of Hello Interview's Top-K
A service runs on several hundred machines. We need the N most frequent request identities across the
over its most recent 24 hours. Examples are the most-searched strings or the most-requested keys of a distributed key-value service.
ranked list of requests and their frequencies
, not a time-series chart and not the KV values. N and K are interchangeable names for the result size.
Video ID, counted once per view.
Request signature, such as a search string or a KV key.
The example assumes a stream of views already exists.
Design logging and collection from the request-serving fleet. This is part of the grading.
Starts with all-time and fixed tumbling hour/day/month windows, then explores sliding windows.
Only the trailing 24 hours. Its endpoint moves with time; arbitrary historical 24-hour queries are not required.
Counting, precomputation, sharding, and fast Top-K reads.
The same principles, with especially strong emphasis on concurrent processing, network efficiency, and correct distributed reduction.
at time T, the conceptual window is
. This is not yesterday's calendar day. The requirement fixes the duration and the fact that the window looks back from the current time; it does not ask for a general historical analytics engine.

“I will start with how each service machine records and exports requests, then distribute counting by request identity. Once each key has a complete count, I will explain rolling expiration, local ranking, and how a small global merge yields the exact result.”
Clarify what exact and last 24 hours mean
collect request occurrences from all participating service machines, grouped by a clearly defined request identity.
return up to N request identities and their counts for the current 24-hour reporting window, in deterministic order.
remove expired counts even during idle periods, survive ordinary component failures, and make missing or stale data visible.
Received attempts, successful responses, logical operations, and user retries count differently.
One occurrence per admitted request attempt at a defined handler boundary. Export retries do not create new occurrences.
Search normalization or including HTTP method/route can merge or split groups.
A versioned canonical request key. Preserve product semantics; do not lowercase or strip fields unless agreed.
Exact frequencies and ranking, or approximation allowed?
Sampling and sketches can lose low-margin winners.
Exact over the admitted, complete input for the reported cutoff. Approximation is a separately negotiated extension.
Can results advance once per minute?
Minute buckets cannot reconstruct the two partial boundary minutes of an arbitrary-second query.
Propose minute-aligned snapshots, updated each minute. The interviewer must accept this relaxation from a continuously moving endpoint.
Collection, lateness, expiry, and publication all consume the budget.
An illustrative healthy-path goal: snapshot age under two minutes; reads P99 under 100ms from an available published snapshot.
Bounds local candidate lists, global merge cost, response size, and caching.
. Return fewer when fewer keys have positive counts.
How large are traffic and distinct-key cardinality?
Requests/s, distinct keys/day, and nonempty key-minute pairs size different resources.
Estimate all three; do not equate hundreds of source machines with a known heap size.
Can a result be stale or partial during failure?
A missing shard can contain the real winner.
Serve the last complete snapshot with its original cutoff if allowed. Do not label a subset-of-shards ranking as the complete fleet answer.
The proposed timing contract is explicit
The worked design reports an exact ranked list for
T is an advertised minute boundary

, not necessarily the wall-clock instant of the API call. Counts are not approximated within that defined window. If the interviewer insists on the literal current-second window, keep finer boundary data and use the extension in

duplicate-safe and durable capture/processing; parallel ingest and counting; bounded memory/log retention; low-impact instrumentation; fast precomputed reads; and observable snapshot freshness/completeness. Scope out arbitrary time ranges, per-user filters, and additional window lengths unless asked.

one logical contribution per captured occurrence; one complete count owner per request key; expiration independent of new arrivals; no negative rolling count; no Top-N truncation before a key's contributions are combined; and one cutoff/configuration for each published global result.
Drive the architecture before choosing the heap
requirements → entities/interface → end-to-end baseline → decision-driven deep dives → final design
. The prompt explicitly wants collection and distributed processing first. Do not spend the first ten minutes coding a max-heap while the logging boundary remains undefined.

Request rate, distinct keys, bucket state, network savings, and merge size.
Occurrence, contribution, rolling count, partition result, global snapshot.

Network reduction, hot keys, exact-second windows, or approximation.
Map the system to requirements and state remaining limits.
What above expectations looks like at IC3

Meet every axis and exceed at least two, including depth or fault tolerance. Volunteer the source-Top-N counterexample, explain why the corrected partition merge is safe, and trace a crash or expiration without double-counting or losing a potential winner.
A clean solution with a defensible exactness boundary beats a more elaborate one built from unexamined “heap,” “Kafka,” and “exactly once” labels.
Size the stream, the key state, and the candidates separately
500 source machines, 2,000 requests/s each, 100M distinct keys in 24 hours, 128 logical counting partitions, and N_max=1,000
. The distinct-key count is a hypothesis to confirm, not a deduction from the machine count. Use decimal units.
Compact raw event example = 32-byte signature + 8-byte time + 16-byte event ID = 56 bytes
Payload = 56 MB/s = 4.8384 TB/day, before framing, key dictionaries and replication
One host sees 120,000 requests/minute. If those requests refer to
, send 6,000 key/count contributions instead of 120,000 occurrences. Retain counts for every distinct key, not only local winners.
At an illustrative 64 bytes/contribution = 3.2 MB/s = 276.48 GB/day
48 hours of that stream, replicated three ways = 1.65888 TB before overhead

This assumes one sealed total per source/key/minute. More frequent partial flushes create more records; with four flushes/minute and every key appearing in all four, the contribution rate can be four times larger. Random unique keys provide little combining benefit. Measure the workload rather than promise a fixed reduction.
Memory: a small Top-N result does not imply small exact state
Ranking nodes, allocator overhead, and exact key bytes/dictionaries are extra.
Sparse history with H=1B nonzero key-minute pairs
H must be measured; it is not determined by U alone. Timestamp/generation and indexes cost more.
1.152 TB for 8-byte counts alone at U=100M.
Use sparse minute maps when most keys are absent in most minutes.
128,000 candidates; about 5.12 MB at 40 bytes each.
At one merge/minute, about 85.33 KB/s average candidate payload, not the full occurrence stream.
About 40 KB of IDs/counts before display strings/framing.
At an illustrative 10K query QPS, roughly 400 MB/s of egress; serving still needs replicas and efficient encoding.
Partition count is not physical machine count.

Several logical partitions can share a worker, sized by measured state, CPU, log throughput, and recovery headroom. Do not launch 128 physical counting machines merely because the stream has 128 partitions.

Retain more than 24 hours of recoverable input when rebuilding a 24-hour window from scratch: allow lateness, recovery delay, and checkpoint age. With reliable snapshots, retain at least the required suffix for restoration; a follower that falls behind the retained suffix must resnapshot.
A small public API; explicit internal identities
Service/namespace, canonical request bytes, signature reference, normalization version. Exact equality is defined by the canonical identity, not just by a possibly colliding hash.
Source timestamp, request key, source/epoch, capture sequence or stable event ID.
Request key, event minute, positive count, source/epoch, durable batch/chunk identity, and routing epoch.
Per-partition sparse minute maps, count per active key, ranking index, current cutoff, and recovery/deduplication positions.
Logical partition ID, configuration epoch, cutoff T, input completeness/version, and sorted local candidates.
Snapshot ID, service scope, window bounds, complete partition manifest, ranked results, and generation time.
The response is ordinary JSON. Clients cannot choose arbitrary
ranges in the base API. Validate N against the declared cap; use
as a total ordering for ties.
The data path is not one HTTP call per occurrence

Source batch (transport envelope):
  source_id, producer_epoch, batch_sequence, destination_partition
  entries: [{ request_key, event_minute, delta_count }]

Logical contribution identity:
  (source_id, producer_epoch, destination_partition, batch_sequence, entry_index)

Partition snapshot:
  (scope, configuration_epoch, cutoff_T, partition_id, revision)
  candidates: [{ request_key, complete_window_count }]

Batch sequences are monotonically increasing within a source epoch and destination logical partition. Preserve envelope/chunk identity across retries. A row's delta is counted once, not once per delivery. Authenticate source publishers and authorize query scopes; frequently requested search strings and keys can contain sensitive information. A hash is not anonymization or an access-control mechanism.
Start with collection, then distribute the expensive work
1. Collect a real stream from the serving fleet

props.aria-label: Request handlers record observations which local exporters deliver into durable ingestion

children.value: Establish where the data comes from. Do not query each search/KV machine at dashboard time and hope their local counters share a consistent window. Export continuously and isolate telemetry transport from serving latency.
a naive raw stream costs one record per request and may overwhelm a central downstream counter. Source combining and partitioned processing will address that.

As a first logical implementation, persist minute counts and query the last 1,440 minutes. This is functionally correct for the agreed cutoff even though a full scan/group/sort is expensive at the target scale.

-- Logical baseline, after aggregation to one row per key and minute.
-- Caller binds start_minute = T - 1440, end_minute = T.
SELECT request_key, SUM(request_count) AS frequency
FROM minute_counts
WHERE scope = :scope
  AND minute_id >= :start_minute
  AND minute_id <  :end_minute
GROUP BY request_key
ORDER BY frequency DESC, request_key ASC
LIMIT :n;
an indexed time filter still touches large numbers of rows and repeatedly recomputes the same result. Note this explicitly; do not claim a timestamp index eliminates aggregation work.
3. Distribute by key, not by source machine

props.aria-label: Source counts are hash-partitioned by request identity into independent counting workers

children.value: A key's occurrences from every source meet at the same logical counting partition. Different keys are counted concurrently. This is the map/combine/shuffle/reduce idea applied continuously.
each owner still needs rolling expiration and ranking, and the query needs a correct global merge. Those are the next mechanisms to explain.
4. Maintain rolling totals and publish a small result

props.aria-label: Per-key rolling counts feed local rankings whose candidates are merged into a cached global result

children.value: Precompute the ranking once per reporting tick rather than once per client query. The serving path becomes cheap and independently scalable. A small replicated merger handles candidates only, not every raw occurrence.

The end-to-end design now reaches the output API. Deep dives will establish why its partition merge is exact, how a key can lose popularity without new traffic, and how replay cannot change a count twice.
Reduce traffic without losing potential winners

The application records the agreed request occurrence with event time and canonical identity. A library can update thread-local/striped counters; a daemon/exporter handles serialization, batching, persistence, compression, and retries. Do not hold a global telemetry lock or wait on remote network I/O in every handler.

Define the durability boundary honestly. Updating only an in-memory counter can lose recent observations on a host crash. If zero capture loss is required, durable capture must precede the business acknowledgment, or use an existing authoritative durable request log. If that latency/cost is unacceptable, negotiate the loss budget; a downstream Kafka replica cannot recover events never recorded.
Combine locally by key and minute

Requests observed on one machine in minute m:
  search("A"), search("A"), search("B"), search("A")

Emit lossless counts for that minute:
  (m, "A", 3)
  (m, "B", 1)

Do NOT emit only the source's Top-1 ("A", 3).
"B" might be common across all the other machines.

Use a sparse map for the current minute and seal it at the boundary. For bursts or high cardinality, flush disjoint chunks earlier with stable chunk IDs; sum each accepted chunk exactly once. Do not send cumulative totals repeatedly unless the protocol explicitly replaces earlier revisions instead of adding them.

For concurrent collection, swap/double-buffer minute state under a short coordination step, then serialize outside the lock. Account for in-flight updates at the boundary. A minute-close signal is not valid while earlier observations can still disappear between buffers.

A batched envelope may contain many keys, but those keys still route to their owners. Split batches by destination partition, or let an ingestion tier repartition them. Batching only by source and keeping all of a host's keys together would leave the same key split across counting owners.

A suitable partitioned log, such as Kafka, gives durable ordered input within each partition, replay, and consumer assignment. The transport produces batches, not one network RPC per key. The application protocol still supplies stable identities for replays across agent restarts.
Request signatures and the output dictionary

A compact signature can reduce repeated long request strings. Keep a canonical identity/dictionary to turn winners back into strings, scoped and retained long enough for replay and serving. Cache known IDs at exporters and send definitions only when necessary.

a 256-bit signature makes accidental collisions very unlikely, not mathematically impossible. For strict exactness, use the canonical key or a collision-resolving dictionary/equality check before combining distinct strings. The hash can route two colliding keys to one partition while their counters remain separate.

Hashing an 8-byte key into 32 bytes increases traffic. Compact IDs or the original key may be better. Normalize only fields the product considers equivalent; otherwise the system answers a different question.
Local Top-N is safe only after complete key aggregation
Suppose N=1. Each source host keeps only its own most frequent request:
The source summaries send A, B, and C. But the true global winner is
. X was not Top-1 on any source. Keeping an arbitrary larger local shortlist does not give a general exactness guarantee either.
, using stable logical partitions and a versioned placement map. All contributions for X reach X's owner, which sees X=270. All A contributions reach A's owner, and so on.
Global Top-N = Top-N of the union of each key partition's Top-N
Preconditions: complete per-key counts; disjoint key ownership;
same time cutoff; same configuration; same deterministic tie order.
If a key is not in its owner's local Top-N, at least N other keys in that partition outrank it. Because that partition holds their
, those same N keys also outrank it globally. Therefore the excluded key cannot be in the global Top-N. A shared tie-breaker makes this argument valid even at equal counts.
With P partitions, the merger needs at most
candidates. It does not need all active keys, the source logs, or the entire history. Replicas of one partition are alternative copies, not extra partitions to add together.
partial across hosts — cannot discard non-winners.
partial across minutes — cannot merge only per-minute Top-N lists either.
complete across all hosts and the whole window — safe to truncate for global merging.
Serving any N up to a cap

Publish each partition's Top-N_max and compute the global Top-N_max once. A request for a smaller N reads a prefix. Use the same total ordering everywhere. If the product changes the cap, rebuild candidate snapshots with the new cap rather than silently infer the missing candidates.
For sorted partition lists, a P-way max-oriented merge can take the first element of each list and advance only the winning list, doing about
merge work with an efficient heap build. Fetching all P×N_max candidates upfront is often simpler at the illustrated small merge size; page them lazily if candidate traffic becomes significant.
Add entering counts. Subtract expiring counts. Advance even when idle.
Let minute IDs be integers. A cutoff T represents the instant at the start of minute T. Store sparse maps
containing total occurrences for each minute after combining all sources assigned to the owner.
C_T(key) = sum B[m][key] for m in [T - W, T)

At T=14:20, the result covers yesterday 14:20 up to, but not including, today 14:20. Advancing to 14:21 adds today's 14:20 minute and removes yesterday's 14:20 minute. It does not reset the whole day.

minute_buckets[minute_id] -> sparse map(request_key -> count)
rolling_totals[request_key] -> count in the current window
ranking_index -> all positive-count keys ordered by (count DESC, key ASC)
cutoff_T -> current complete reporting boundary
input_positions + deduplication_state + checkpoint_generation

advance_one_minute(T):
    entering = minute_buckets.get(T, empty_map)
    leaving  = minute_buckets.get(T - 1440, empty_map)
    affected = keys(entering) UNION keys(leaving)

    for key in affected:
        old = rolling_totals.get(key, 0)
        new = old + entering.get(key, 0) - leaving.get(key, 0)
        require new >= 0
        replace ranking entry (old, key) with (new, key)
        delete zero-count totals/rank entries

    retire expired bucket T - 1440 when recovery policy allows
    checkpoint/record advancement to T + 1
    emit immutable partition result for cutoff T + 1

This is algorithmic pseudocode, not a storage transaction implementation. The state, advancement position, and consumed input must be recoverable together; otherwise a restart can subtract the same expired minute twice.
Do not rescan every key to expire time

An expiration schedule or timestamped ring buffer tells the worker exactly which minute leaves. Visit keys in the entering and leaving buckets, not every key in the dictionary. The approximate cost per tick is proportional to those bucket memberships and their ranking updates.
A ring slot must carry its absolute minute ID/generation. Slot

alone is unsafe when late/future data and wrapped slots coexist. Keep pending/future buckets separately or enough guarded slots; never overwrite still-needed history simply because two timestamps have the same modulo.

If a key had one million requests 24 hours ago and no requests now, it must drop in rank when those requests expire. Expiration triggered only when a new request for that key arrives gives the wrong answer. Checkpointed timers or scheduled ticks are required.

A not-yet-finalized minute can accept deduplicated late contributions. If an explicitly authorized correction falls inside the current window, update its bucket and rolling total, refresh the affected ranking, and publish a new snapshot revision only after a coherent recomputation. A late contribution outside the current window must not inflate its current count.

A closed source-minute manifest promises no further ordinary contributions for that minute. Unexpected later data is a protocol violation or a backfill, not an excuse to quietly change a supposedly complete snapshot. Define whether to rebuild, publish a correction revision, or reject with an observable error.
The heap is an index, not the whole system
. A current winner can expire and be replaced by a key that received no new traffic. Maintain a way to find that next candidate.
Ordered set/tree over all active keys
Keep a count map and entries ordered by count plus deterministic key tie-break. Remove the old entry and insert the new one on changes.
O(log U_p) per changed key, about O(log U_p + N) traversal for Top-N, and O(U_p) ranking state per partition.
Indexed max-heap over all active keys
Maintain key-to-heap-position handles. Repair up/down after increment or decrement.
O(log U_p) updates. Top-N enumeration needs extra work, such as a frontier over the heap; array positions are not ranks.
Min-heap of N winners + full count map
Scan all counts at each publication and retain the best N in the heap.
Simple and correct; O(U_p log N) work per refresh. Useful if it fits the measured cadence, not if it burns the whole fleet every minute.
Only a min-heap of the N current winners
Not sufficient for the exact sliding problem on its own.
After winners decay, it cannot identify the best excluded key unless additional state/search is retained.
Lazy heap with old versioned entries
Discard obsolete entries when popped and retain authoritative counts/expiry state.
Needs bounded garbage collection/rebuilds; stale versions can otherwise grow without bound and damage tail latency.
Why the supplied lazy-refresh sketch needs care

Being the 1,000th element in a heap array does not make a key the 1,000th-ranked request. A heap guarantees a parent/child ordering, not a fully sorted prefix. Expiration can change keys anywhere in the structure, even if a new request touches only one node.

A specialized lazy-decay heap may be possible with valid bounds and a proof, but “refresh the first thousand and the swapped nodes” is not that proof. The simpler interview answer is an explicit expiry schedule plus ordinary point updates to the ranking index.
State size follows active identities and history

histories, not a timestamped object per occurrence when minute-aligned windows suffice. U_p is the number of active distinct keys owned by a partition; H_p is its nonempty key-minute history. Exact state is roughly

Use memory for hot counts/ranking and an appropriate local persisted/checkpointed state store for history if needed. A stream processor's state backend or an existing KV engine can support this; do not invent a bespoke disk heap unless its advantage is needed and defensible. Spill/load behavior must still meet the refresh budget.
A global merge needs one time and one input boundary
Even perfectly computed partition candidates produce an inconsistent answer if half describe 14:20 and half 14:21. The merger selects a
with a manifest of logical partitions.
When is a minute safe to publish?

Sources/exporters can publish ordered close markers or manifests identifying the last batch/chunk for each destination partition, including explicit empty-minute progress. A collector advances a source's frontier only after every required preceding chunk is durably received. The expected producer/source set comes from a versioned membership/lifecycle contract.

Owners process their data and closure progress, expire through the agreed T, and emit an immutable candidate snapshot. The coordinator publishes only when all expected partitions report the same T/configuration and their input boundaries satisfy the policy.

This metadata is batched progress information, not a centralized RPC per occurrence. A source that terminates cleanly seals its last interval; an unexpected lost source cannot simply be declared empty to preserve a green dashboard.
Watermarks are not magical completeness certificates

A bound such as “wait 30 seconds for late events” is an operational assumption. It does not prove that an offline host had no unseen traffic. Distinguish exact ranking of complete admitted input from exact counting of every real request that may have occurred on an unreachable machine.
. Retries replace the same identity instead of becoming additional contributions.
A merger verifies the full partition manifest, combines lists under the shared tie order, and stores an immutable GlobalSnapshot.
Publish a small latest-complete pointer atomically after the snapshot is available. Do not update a ranked list entry-by-entry where readers can see half an old result and half a new one.
Query-service replicas fetch the latest complete snapshot from a cache or durable snapshot store and return its real bounds, generation time, and status.

The merger is small enough to replicate or run with a fenced active publisher and standby. Even though it is a final aggregation stage, it is not the forbidden single machine that receives and counts the full raw stream.

If a worker lags, retain the last complete snapshot and its original window_end. Serve it only within the agreed stale-result policy or return unavailable. If offering an explicitly incomplete diagnostic result, label it as such; it cannot be represented as the exact Top-N of the entire service.

The latest-complete pointer must not move backward when a slow merger finishes an older generation. Compare cutoff/configuration/revision or enforce one authoritative publisher. Cache TTL alone does not solve mixed-generation publication.
Replication protects input; checkpoints protect interpretation

Use a replicated durable log for accepted contribution batches, with a documented acknowledgment policy and failure-domain placement. Counting workers checkpoint their minute history, current cutoff, rolling counts, deduplication progress, and input offsets consistently. The ranking index may be included or rebuilt from authoritative totals.

Source batch B contains (minute 5000, key X, delta 17).
1. The broker durably accepts B; the ACK is lost.
2. The source retries B with the SAME identity.
3. Owner applies its logical contribution once, not twice.
4. Owner crashes after updating state but before a durable checkpoint.
5. Restore checkpoint + input position together, then replay the suffix.
6. Rebuild ranking/expiry state and publish only after catch-up.

For the batched protocol, keep a durable contiguous applied-sequence watermark per source epoch and destination partition, with bounded gap tracking if out-of-order chunks are accepted. Apply each logical batch once within the checkpoint/recovery protocol. This can avoid retaining a separate deduplication entry for every raw request. An old source epoch beyond retained retry history must use an explicit recovery/backfill procedure, not silently replay as fresh data.

If state and source offsets cannot commit atomically in the chosen stack, use a proven checkpoint/replay mechanism or idempotent state updates. Kafka producer idempotence within its supported session does not by itself deduplicate every application-level replay or external sink write.
Resume its durable spool/capture log with stable identities. Mark unsealed input as incomplete until recovered or handled under an explicit loss policy.
A replica downstream cannot recover observations that existed only in the lost process's RAM.
Bounded local spool, exponential backoff, jitter, and rate-limited replay.
Finite disk cannot buffer an unlimited outage. Do not silently drop counts and still claim exact completeness.
Use its replication/failover protocol and the configured durable ACK. Retry uncertain writes using the same identities.
Do not acknowledge a weaker replica set while pretending the old durability guarantee still holds.
Reassign its logical partition, restore snapshot/state, replay, and catch up time expiration. Fence the old owner's candidate publication.
An empty restarted heap is not a recovered 24-hour count.
Apply every required enter/expire transition, or rebuild the current window from retained buckets, before publishing a new candidate set.
Do not expire just one minute and label the result as current.
Rebuild from persisted partition snapshots; serve the last complete global snapshot from redundant storage/servers where policy allows.
A cache is not the only durable record of the result or the counting state.
A whole logical partition is unavailable
Keep the complete old result or fail the fresh request; surface the delayed partition.
Merging P-1 partitions can miss the actual winner and cannot be called globally exact.
Log retention no longer covers recovery
Restore a newer valid snapshot or reconstruct from a retained authoritative source; disclose any unrecoverable gap.
Cannot reconstruct 24 hours from only the last hour of data and an empty checkpoint.

One consumer group typically distributes logical counting partitions among workers. Additional replicas/standbys must receive or restore the same state intentionally; running a few independent processes and load-balancing queries does not guarantee matching counts.

Monitor capture drops, source closure lag, oldest spool entry, broker lag, active-key/history size, expiration lag, negative-count invariant failures, checkpoint/recovery age, candidate-generation completeness, and published snapshot age. A negative count should fail validation and trigger repair, not be clamped to zero to hide a replay bug.
How can we further reduce network and resources?
Repeated requests become a single counted contribution before crossing the network.
Must retain all distinct source keys and preserve the time resolution. Benefit falls for unique-key traffic.
Avoid repeated long strings, per-message framing, connection churn, and tiny writes.
Need dictionary/collision correctness. A 32-byte hash can be larger than the original short key.
Repeated keys/minutes and small counts compress well; fewer bytes to brokers and replicas.
Consumes CPU and can add batching latency. Benchmark end-to-end rather than maximizing compression ratio alone.
Touch only entering/leaving key memberships instead of rescanning the whole day.
Requires bucket/history state and consistent recovery of the current cutoff.
Only bounded candidate lists cross into the merger, regardless of raw event volume.
Safe only after complete key aggregation, with shared cutoff/configuration/ties.
Many read requests reuse the same result; API nodes never query every worker per request.
Freshness is the snapshot cadence plus processing lag, and must be exposed.
Less fan-in pressure and unnecessary candidate transfer for very large P.
Each level must merge disjoint complete key partitions for one generation. Source-local truncated lists remain unsafe.
Only nonempty key-minute pairs need entries; expired data and stale checkpoints can be removed safely.
Retain recovery and late-data headroom. High-cardinality traffic still requires substantial exact state.

Sampling the source stream, dropping low-frequency keys, retaining only per-host Top-N, or keeping an arbitrary larger candidate list can all save resources while changing the problem. They require approximation permission or a proven exact pruning bound.

“My first savings are lossless: local key/minute combining, compact batched records, incremental expiry, and merging only complete-key candidates. If the exact state is still too expensive, I would negotiate approximation and an error contract rather than silently omit rare requests.”
Partition the work that is actually saturated
More exporters/brokers and counting capacity; larger efficient batches; maintain replay headroom.
Increasing raw R does not always increase distinct-key state U by the same factor.
More distinct keys or key-minute pairs
More logical/state partitions, compact sparse history, and a suitable persisted state backend.
N can stay at 100 while exact state grows by 100×. Ranking result size is not a state-size bound.
One request key is extremely popular
Local source combining often collapses millions of occurrences into at most one total per source/minute.
If still hot, use an intermediate salted partial-count stage, then recombine the full key before final ranking. Ranking salted fragments independently breaks the proof.
One partition has too many keys
Use many virtual partitions, workload-aware assignment, and safe split/migration.
Move the full relevant history, totals, retry state, input positions, and expiration position, not just the heap's winners.
Replicate stateless APIs/caches and immutable result storage; cache dictionary lookups for displayed keys.
Output bytes and cache stampedes matter even though computing one result is cheap.
Cap N, use P-way/paged/hierarchical merge, and measure publication latency.
The final stage can become a bottleneck eventually; it is acceptable here because it receives bounded summaries, not raw events.

Maintain a routing/configuration epoch and logical owner identities. Prepare new owners from a snapshot and replay suffix, establish a cutover barrier, then publish candidates for the new partition manifest only after they are ready. Retired owners cannot submit a second valid copy of the same key range to the same generation.

Increasing the physical node count need not change key-to-logical-partition mapping. If changing that mapping, use the same migration contract; do not rehash live producers independently and assume history follows.

If a tested worker can apply 50K representative contribution/expiry operations per second at the target state size, use that measurement with a utilization target and failure headroom. Do not claim a fixed generic “Kafka QPS” or “heap machine QPS” independent of payload, bucket cardinality, and checkpoint work.

For 10×/100× scale, distinguish traffic growth, key/history growth, and read growth. Add tiers/cells only where the workload requires them. A replicated small publisher may remain adequate even when counting expands dramatically, because its input is P×N rather than R.
An annotated whiteboard you can explain from
recovery and configuration. The annotations deliberately show the source record, shard key, rolling state, expiration rule, and global merge conditions.
Logical components, not one required deployment per box. Kafka/Redis are illustrative implementations.
Rolling Top-N requests: annotated interview whiteboard

Request-serving machines export lossless key-minute counts into a durable stream partitioned by request identity. Counting owners keep sparse minute history, complete rolling counts, and a ranking index for all active keys. Timed expiration removes old counts even when idle. Owners publish candidate lists for the same cutoff and configuration; a replicated merger creates an immutable global Top-N snapshot served through a cache and API. The diagram includes record schemas, recovery state, and a warning that source-local Top-N lists are not sufficient.

Explain collection first, then the partition proof, the expiration rule, exact snapshot publication, and the network savings.

The source/partition distinction is visible in one picture. The final merger sees bounded candidate lists; every counting owner sees complete counts for its assigned keys. Replicated checkpoints and exact publication prevent failover from silently changing the answer.
Why each component earned its place

The exporter isolates capture/transport and reduces duplicate key traffic; the durable log supports replay and distribution; the owners hold complete key-window state; the ranking index makes candidate extraction cheap; the small merger provides one coherent result; and the snapshot cache separates read QPS from computation. None is introduced merely to make the architecture look larger.
Follow one request identity from three hosts to an expiring winner
During minute m, hosts H1/H2/H3 see request X 90 times each, alongside their own host-specific request 100 times each.
Each host emits all key/minute totals, including X=90. These are six logical contributions, not a host-local Top-1 summary.
The keyed stream routes all X contributions to the same owner. That owner's bucket contains
; A/B/C each have 100 at their respective owners.
A retried H2 chunk retains its ID. X remains 270, not 360.
Each owner includes the minute when advancing its agreed cutoff. The global merge sees X's complete count and correctly returns X ahead of A/B/C.
Exactly 24 hours later, minute m leaves. Its owner's expiration timer subtracts 270 for X even if X has had no recent traffic.
If another key Y now has the largest positive count, its ranking entry is still available and it can become the winner without receiving a new request at that moment.
Use a three-minute window for a compact example; the production mechanism uses W=1,440.
m0: A=100; m1: B=80; m2: empty
A=0, B=80 → B wins, despite no new B request.

This example exposes why expiration cannot depend on new arrivals and why retaining only the old winner is insufficient. Empty minutes advance time; they are not reasons to leave yesterday's counts unchanged.
Adapt the design when an assumption changes
What if the last 24 hours must end at the exact current second?

Minute totals lose the location of events inside the earliest and latest partial minute. You cannot answer that literal window exactly from minute buckets alone. Keep finer-grained observations for the relevant boundaries, or use exact timestamped occurrence counts with expiration timers. A one-second bucket contract is another negotiated resolution, not arbitrary-instant exactness.

You must also align all partition computations to the requested T and the same input completeness boundary. Precomputed per-minute winners may no longer suffice when boundary corrections change ranks; owners need the ability to recompute candidates against the exact corrected window. This costs more memory, expiration work, coordination, and potentially read latency.
Can we use Count-Min Sketch or another approximate structure?

Only if approximate counts/ranking and the error contract are acceptable. Count-Min Sketch estimates a queried key's frequency; it does not enumerate all candidate keys by itself. Pair it with an appropriate heavy-hitter/candidate mechanism and define window aging, confidence/error bounds, and how close-ranked keys can be misordered.

A lifetime insertion-only sketch is not a rolling 24-hour solution. Aged window sketches or a carefully supported decrement protocol are required. Candidate tracking under expirations is itself nontrivial. Do not claim a sketch plus an arbitrary fixed shortlist preserves exact winners.
What if every request is a new unique string?

Local combining provides almost no reduction, active cardinality approaches occurrences retained, and nearly all counts tie at one. Exact arbitrary queryable identities still cost state and transport; the known N bound does not let you silently discard identities whose future repetition could make them winners. Add capacity, use a justified exact strategy for the altered workload, or negotiate approximation/limits explicitly.
Why not poll all source machines when a query arrives?

It couples read availability/latency to every source, duplicates aggregation work per query, and makes shared cutoffs and changing membership difficult. It can be a simple low-scale diagnostic, but the prompt asks for continuous collection and concurrent processing, not a fan-out query over the live serving fleet.
Why not merge Top-N for each minute of the last day?

The same partial-count trap applies across time. A key can be just below every minute's local winners while having the highest sum over 24 hours. Aggregate the full key-window count before truncating, unless using a proven bound-based multi-pass pruning algorithm.
What if one key is so hot that its reducer is a bottleneck?

First use source-side counting: a popular key no longer causes one cross-network update per occurrence. If that is insufficient, count salted partials in parallel, then sum those partials into one complete key count before ranking. Do not merge Top-N of the salted fragments as though each fragment were a globally complete key.
Can an owner skip sending an unchanged candidate list?

It can reuse an immutable candidate payload, but it must still certify that payload for the new cutoff and completeness generation. Otherwise the merger cannot distinguish “unchanged after correct expiration” from “worker stuck and no longer expiring data.” Count changes for existing winners still matter even if their identities do not change.
Would a second delayed consumer be simpler for expiration?

An increment stream plus a consumer delayed by 24 hours can generate decrements, but it still needs correct event-time alignment, retention beyond the delay, duplicate-safe processing, and recovery of both positions. Broker arrival time differs from event time under delayed export. A sparse minute expiration schedule is often easier to explain for the agreed snapshot contract.
Can we put all counts in Redis or a database sorted set?

An ordered set is a useful primitive, but one global instance recreates the central state/write bottleneck. Partition complete keys, maintain expirations and recoverability, and make counts and rank updates consistent. Check the implementation's numeric limits, tie semantics, and recovery behavior instead of assuming the product name supplies them.
What if the service spans datacenters?

Aggregate locally to reduce cross-colo traffic, but send every partial key count to a stage that computes the full global key total before ranking. Replicate durable input/checkpoints and define what happens to freshness/completeness when a colo is unreachable. Summing overlapping replica totals or excluding a colo silently gives the wrong fleet answer.
Can we support multiple window lengths or arbitrary historical queries later?

Several fixed trailing windows can share base minute buckets while maintaining separate totals and expiration boundaries, at higher memory/CPU cost. Arbitrary start/end windows require sufficient historical counts and a different query planning/aggregation budget. Do not pretend the one current rolling total can answer every historical range.
What to say as you draw
These are short transitions. Leave room for the interviewer to redirect, and adapt the timing/exactness contract rather than defending an assumption they reject.

“This is distributed frequency ranking for one trailing 24-hour window. I would clarify the request identity, whether retries count as new attempts, exact versus approximate results, and whether a minute-aligned result refreshed every minute is acceptable.”

“I will instrument the service boundary and export timestamped request counts through a durable, batched pipeline. Repeated occurrences of the same key in a minute can be combined locally, but I must keep every distinct key. I will not send only each machine's Top-N.”

“The stream is partitioned by request identity, not the source host. All occurrences of X from the fleet reach one logical owner. That lets different keys be counted concurrently while ensuring each local ranking uses complete global counts.”

“Each owner keeps sparse minute counts, a rolling total for each active key, and an ordered ranking index. At a minute boundary it adds the new minute and subtracts the minute that just left the 24-hour window. Timers do this even when no new traffic arrives.”

“Now local Top-N is safe: a key excluded from its owner's Top-N already has N complete-count keys ahead of it, so it cannot be a global winner. I merge at most P times N candidates using the same cutoff and tie order. That proof would not hold for Top-N from the original source machines.”

“I publish an immutable result only after all expected partitions have candidates for one complete generation. Workers restore counts, expiry position, and input offsets together, then replay duplicate-safely. If a partition is unavailable, I keep the labeled last complete snapshot rather than report a false fresh winner.”

“The big lossless savings are local combining, compact and compressed batches, sparse expiry state, bounded candidate transfer, and precomputing once for many readers. Approximation is a separate product trade-off, not something I would introduce by silently dropping rare keys.”

“The distributed work is on the high-volume path; the central merge sees only small complete-key summaries. The remaining trade-offs are exact-state memory, the agreed snapshot resolution/freshness, and the capture/recovery guarantees. I would scale the saturated resource rather than just adding more heaps.”
Keep the useful ideas; challenge unsupported shortcuts
Unsafe: a globally frequent key can lose on every source. Combine by identity first, then truncate.
“We only need the N winners in memory.”
Expirations can promote excluded keys without new requests. Keep exact active-key/history state or an equivalent correct search structure.
“The first 1,000 heap nodes are the first 1,000 ranks.”
A heap is not a fully sorted array. Use explicit expiry updates or prove a specialized lazy scheme's invariants.
“We decrement when a new request arrives.”
Old counts expire even during silence. Drive advancement with recoverable timers/progress.
“A minute ring means exact right-now answers.”
It is exact for minute-aligned boundaries only; arbitrary-second windows need boundary information.
“Hashing to 32 bytes makes it exact and smaller.”
Clarify collision handling and original-key recovery. Short keys may grow when hashed; hashes are not anonymization.
“Replicate the heap on a few machines and load balance.”
Define input delivery, ownership, checkpoints, replay, and the served generation. Independently running replicas can otherwise diverge.
“All partitions replied, so the input is complete.”
A source may still be delayed or lost. Partition snapshots also need input-frontier/source completeness semantics.
“A timestamp index avoids all expensive SQL work.”
It narrows time but still leaves grouping/ranking across many keys. Incremental totals and precomputation remove repeated work.
“The final merger is a single counter, so the design fails.”
Not if it sees only P×N bounded summaries and has failover. Avoid centralizing the full occurrence stream, not every final coordination step.

When a hint challenges your approach, explain which assumption changes and adjust the design. You can say “That shortcut would work if counts were already partition-complete; on source hosts it loses candidates. I will move the Top-N step after the key-based reduction.” This is collaborative reasoning, not arguing with the interviewer.

Clarifies and sketches before details; proactively discovers issues; resolves them with a correct distributed answer and minimal unnecessary computation/network overhead.

Dives into one part, struggles to connect the system, needs major issues pointed out, and has difficulty distributing work or preserving accurate counts.
Ignores major surfaces, needs help identifying and solving most issues, and cannot progress beyond sending everything to one counting machine.

The generic wording in some notes refers to “exceptions”; the counted items in this question are request occurrences. Focus on the intended distribution and counting signals, not that incidental wording.

means passing every axis and exceeding at least two, one of which is depth or fault tolerance. Complete the design with minimal hints and leave time for several follow-ups. Meets Expectations passes all axes with level-appropriate hints; Exceeds Expectations exceeds four or more axes with additional insight.
No field guide guarantees a score. The strongest preparation is being able to derive the partition proof and expiration behavior yourself, then adapt when the interviewer changes the assumptions.

Collect durably. Combine losslessly. Partition complete keys. Expire by time. Rank all active candidates. Merge one coherent generation. Serve a small snapshot. Make every approximation or loss boundary explicit.
